questions.prompt: How does Andreyev redefine consonance and dissonance for musical motion?
choices: B Consonance ≈ stable (needn’t move); dissonance creates need for movement/resolution.
C Dissonance is forbidden in Western music.
D Consonance only exists in electronic music.
questions.explain: He rejects pretty/ugly; stability vs need-to-move is the working distinction.

questions.prompt: Dividing a vibrating string in half (2:1) yields which interval above the fundamental?
questions.explain: Half the string → 2:1 ratio → octave (frequency doubles).

questions.prompt: What is a half (imperfect) cadence in his I–IV–V discussion?
choices: A Ending on I after V–I with maximum finality.
B Arriving on V (dominant) as a provisional resting place, not yet home.
C Only IV–I in Renaissance style.
D Any cadence that uses exclusively diminished triads.
questions.explain: Moving to V and stopping is a half/imperfect cadence—temporary, not home.

questions.prompt: A deceptive (interrupted) cadence typically moves from:
choices: B V to VI (e.g., G to A in C major).
questions.explain: Deceptive/interrupted cadence: V→VI, thwarting the expected V→I.

questions.prompt: What motion defines the plagal cadence he associates with early music?
choices: B IV to I (subdominant to tonic)—a weaker close than V–I.
questions.explain: Plagal cadence = IV→I; associated with medieval/Renaissance practice; weaker than authentic V–I.
